subject: significant detection covariates in a dsm

messages.author: 5e426c478a162ca8
messages.subject: significant detection covariates in a dsm
parts:
Hello again, I've had a somewhat interesting development in my density surface modelling for arctic songbirds. While trying to deal with the problem of overdispersion by adding potentially missing covariates to the model, I included a couple of the covariates actually used in the fitting of my candidate set of detection functions. In particular, start time of survey popped out as being highly significant in my dsm. Start time was not a significant covariate in my detection function modelling. In my survey design I sampled at all hours of the day (although mostly between mid morning and afternoon) assuming that due to the near 24 hour daylight for most of the summer and published research on the subject, that the typical daily activity patterns for songbirds (and other avian species) would be relaxed in the arctic (also because of the necessity of fitting sampling protocol in between other aspects of our research program). 

It seems to me this is a pretty important catch. That start time of survey was not important in the fitting of the detection function but was important in the dsm to me indicates that it probably caused birds to not be detected at all in some of my surveys. Non-counts obviously cannot be adjusted with a detection function, and so not taking this into account (or not designing your sampling protocol properly), could lead to zero inflation of your dataset and cause you to very much underestimate true abundance. Is my reading of this situation plausible? Is including detection covariates in a density surface model fair game? 

As a side note, i also fit a zero inflated mixture model to my data, including start time in both the main and zero inflated portion of the model - start time was only significant in the zero inflated portion of the model, which seems to fit with my intuition so far. 

Interested to hear someone's take on this who has more knowledge/experience than me.

Kevin

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] significant detection covariates in a dsm
parts:
Kevin, that is likely the case.  For species that are mostly detected by song, if some individuals stop singing for periods during the day, they are likely to be undetected during such periods.  In theory, if you’re still certain to detect them on the line or at the point, all should be OK, but if quiet birds move away from the observer, they may well escape detection.  Similarly, females are often undetected.  For temperate songbird surveys, it is often a good strategy to carry out surveys at peak singing season, at times of day when song is greatest, and to record only singing males, with a view to estimating the number of territories.

 

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 5e426c478a162ca8
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] significant detection covariates in a dsm
parts:
Hi Steve, just to reopen this, I've been doing some reading, mostly from cetacean studies where detection on the transect line is often not 100% and varies based on weather conditions (Beaufort sea state in their cases). This seems like pretty much the exact same thing going on in my avian study, where even after correction via detection function, there are still large differences between survey counts on the basis of weather conditions, time of day, etc. Barlow (2015) appeared to tackle this issue simply by including Beafort sea state in his presence-absence model (he was trying to estimate relative g(0) for each Beaufort level) - is that approach valid for application to a count model? Or is there a need to partition the analysis such that the unaccounted for detection covariates only apply to the zeros in the data? Basically I'm asking if a two stage modelling approach with presence-absence followed by poisson or whatever is necessary, or if i can stick with my current negative binomial model.

My apologies for asking so many questions lately. I'm in the late stages of my study, so i'm trying to make sure all the i's are dotted and t's are crossed analysis-wise.

Thanks again,
Kevin

messages.author: 7482eee8d2863d12
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] significant detection covariates in a dsm
parts:
Hi Kevin, List,

In case it's useful, we did something like this in a recent paper
modelling abundance of a small porpoise, the vaquita.
(https://doi.org/10.1111/conl.12331 -- technical details are in the
supplemental materials.) There were a few differences: it was a
one-stage (Bayesian) model rather than two-stage; we modelled g0
affecting count rather than presence-absence; there were a few other
complications.

The danger in such models, where we put detectability variables into the
count or presence-absence model, is that if there is a correlation
between these variables and animal density then we have confounding
between detectability and density, and it is difficult to see how
density can be accurately inferred. For example, if g0 is affected by
some habitat variable in your bird study such as vegetation type (birds
tend to sing in one type and not others, and you only detect birds
aurally), and so is density, then putting habitat type in as a covariate
will not allow you to accurately estimate density. g0 must be inferred
some other way (e.g., by a double-observer method). Hope this makes sense.

Cheers, Len

messages.author: 5e426c478a162ca8
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] significant detection covariates in a dsm
parts:
Thanks Len, I'll dig into your paper. 

Yes this complication has struck me too. Specifically in my models day of the year is highly significant, but potentially modelling both g(0) and true abundance (birds singing less as the season goes along, females virtually undetectable when on eggs). I dont only detect by sound, since I'm on the tundra with pretty good visibility, but even so... That's likely just a confounder I'll have to admit up front, cause I dont see any way around it at the moment. the other covariates (weather, start time) don't really suffer from this problem.
